audio_caption: A male speaker begins talking in a calm, informative tone about why Polaris doesn't move, or more accurately, almost doesn't move. He mentions discussing the heliocentric and galactic models.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing the composition of galaxies, stating that "our galaxy consists of hundreds of millions of stars" and explains that our sun is one of them. He emphasizes that all stars visible to the naked eye are from our galaxy, the Milky Way. He continues to explain that our sun and other stars rotate around the galactic center, and that the position between the stars relative to each other "stays the same, more or less." He also acknowledges that the stars have some movement, but that "this can't be tracked with normal equipment."

The audio clip begins with a male speaker explaining that "in our solar system" the Earth's "rotational axis also stays the same," and that "this is why we have seasons" due to the Earth's "tilt." He continues by explaining that "this tilt is always directed to the polar star," clarifying that it's "the celestial pole which doesn't change its orientation." He notes that "it does change its orientation, but only slightly." Concluding that "it's better to say it almost doesn't change its orientation."

The audio begins with a man speaking in an informational and educational tone, explaining the Earth's tilt in December and June, causing different seasons in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. He states, "in December, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the sun, and the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the sun. This is because the Northern Hemisphere now has winter, and the Southern Hemisphere has summer." The speaker notes that "exactly, the opposite is in June," emphasizing the consistent tilt and Earth's different position on its orbit around the sun. The audio concludes with an "Uhm".

The audio begins with a male speaker explaining that Polaris does not stay in the exact same place, and elaborates on stars rotating around the center of the galaxy and their independent movements. He speaks in an informative tone. He then states that it takes a long time to see differences in constellations, which can only be observed using "really precise instruments."

A male speaker explains a reason why Polaris doesn't stay in the same place, stating "another reason", "not staying at the exact same place". He says that the rotation axis does not stay exactly the same, and that there is a movement called precession which causes the rotation axis to change its tilt, noting that it is not always 23.3 degrees. The speaker has a measured, explanatory tone.

The clip begins with a male speaker discussing something that is not visible to the naked eye, but can be recognized with instruments accessible to amateur astronomers, like Star Trackers. He explains that Star Trackers need to be "polar aligned" and that these devices rotate 15 degrees per hour to compensate for the Earth's rotation. This helps the camera stay at the exact same point despite the Earth's rotation, which requires "a polar alignment" with the Star Tracker. He elaborates, explaining one must look through a scope and point at Polaris. He repeats and pauses, "There, we see."

The audio clip features a male speaker discussing the complexities of polar alignment in astronomy, pointing out that simply aiming at a star isn't accurate because the star "is not at the celestial pole," further mentioning the specific star, Polaris, and its "certain distance" from the celestial pole. The speaker uses a calm, informative tone.

A male speaker describes a crosshair marking the celestial pole and a ring around it, explaining that it's used to position the polar star depending on the time of day and year. He adds that the ring accounts for earth's rotation. He mentions multiple rings indicate the polar star's changing distance to the celestial pole. Speaking tone is informative and focused.

The audio begins with someone, likely a male speaker, describing apps used for polar alignment, which help determine position on Earth and time, along with the correct position of Polaris, or the Northern Star, on a ring. The speaker's tone is matter-of-fact, almost technical. The audio concludes, with the speaker about to say "and" before the clip cuts off.

The audio clip features one male speaker who explains the benefits of polar aligning a Star Tracker with an app, enabling long exposures to photograph faint objects not visible to the naked eye. He emphasizes the ability to "catch more light" and make objects visible, describing this as a "really interesting aspect of astrophotography." His tone is calm and informative.

A male speaker with a calm and explanatory tone introduces the term "circumpolar stars" and explains they are dependent on the location on Earth. These stars rotate around a celestial pole and never dip below the horizon. The speaker clarifies these stars may be above the horizon during the day but are not visible. As you move closer to the celestial pole, more constellations never dip beyond the horizon. At the equator, where celestial poles may be visible, there are no circumpolar constellations because they move around and vanish beyond the horizon after half a day. He further elaborates that you won't find northern circumpolar constellations in the southern hemisphere or southern ones in the northern hemisphere, as they are never visible there.

The clip features a single male speaker, explaining the concept of seasonal constellations and their relation to the Earth's orbit around the sun. He speaks in a conversational and informative tone. The speaker mentions that the constellations visible in the night sky depend on the seasons because the sun's light obscures stars behind it. Then the speaker mentions "different seasonal constellations, because you see to the Earth, to the opposite side".
The clip features a single male speaker discussing "a difference of a solar day and a sidereal day" in a neutral tone.

The clip begins with a male speaker, in an informative tone, describing a solar day. He explains the difference between solar days, normal days, and Sidereal days, relative to the movement of the stars, resulting in an additional rotation per year due to earth's orbit. In closing, he thanks the listener and bids goodbye.
